title: NRI Capital Gains: When the Basic Exemption Limit Can — and Cannot — Cut Your Tax
excerpt: The ₹2.5 lakh exemption shelters an NRI's interest and rental income, but it cannot be set off against long-term capital gains on property — a resident-only benefit that catches many sellers out.
body:
• An NRI cannot use an unused basic exemption limit to reduce long-term capital gains on property taxed under Section 112 — that set-off is reserved for residents, so the entire gain is taxable.
  • The exemption limit (₹2.5 lakh under the old regime) can still shelter slab-rate income such as NRO interest or rent, and short-term gains that are themselves taxed at slab rates.
  • NRIs also get no Section 87A rebate — the benefit that takes resident tax to zero at higher incomes does not apply to non-residents at any age.
  • On a property sale to an NRI seller, the buyer must deduct TDS under Section 195 — around 20% on long-term gains — so filing an Indian return is usually needed to recover any excess.

It is one of the most common and costly misunderstandings in NRI tax planning: the assumption that if your total Indian income is small, the basic exemption limit will wipe out the tax on a property sale. For long-term capital gains, it will not. The Outlook Money tax clinic states the rule plainly: a non-resident is not entitled to set off a shortfall in the basic exemption limit against long-term capital gains, so an NRI with no other Indian income pays tax on the entire gain.

Where the exemption limit still works

The basic exemption limit is not useless to NRIs — it just does not reach capital gains taxed under the special-rate sections. It applies first against income taxed at slab rates: NRO account interest, rental income, and short-term gains on assets such as property held under 24 months, which are also taxed at slab rates. Advisers are divided on one edge case — whether a leftover exemption can then be applied to long-term gains on listed equity under Section 112A. A detailed CA Sahuja guide to AY 2025–26 filings says the adjustment is not available to NRIs against gains under Sections 112 or 112A, while some practitioner guides allow it for 112A after other income is exhausted. On short-term equity gains under Section 111A there is no dispute: the set-off is residents-only.

The other resident-only benefits

Two related traps catch returning Indians and new NRIs. First, the Section 87A rebate — worth up to ₹25,000 under the old regime and far more under the new — is restricted to resident individuals; NRIs pay slab tax from the first rupee above the exemption limit. Second, the higher exemption limits for senior and super-senior citizens under the old regime (₹3 lakh and ₹5 lakh) also apply only to residents, so an NRI parent's Indian income is measured against ₹2.5 lakh regardless of age.

What to do before you sell

Because the buyer of an NRI's property must deduct TDS under Section 195 at roughly 20% of the gain on a long-term sale, the cash-flow hit arrives before the return is filed. NRIs with a genuinely low final liability can apply for a lower-deduction certificate before the sale, and should file an Indian ITR for the year of sale to claim any refund. Timing also matters: spreading a family's disposals across financial years, and using the Section 54 and 54EC reinvestment exemptions where available, are legal ways to cut a bill that the exemption limit cannot.
